ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The Volcano Park has always been one of the popular tourist attractions in Tengchong, and hot air balloon tours have become a new type of tourism activity. As shown in the figure, tourists ascend to a certain height in the gondola with the hot air balloon, and the breathtaking scenery of rolling seas of clouds and radiant clouds around the park leaves people in awe. From a physics perspective, the hot air balloon is a marvelous demonstration of some fundamental forces on Earth. Initially, the hot air balloon is anchored to the ground, and the air inside is slowly heated, causing its density to continuously decrease. When heated to a certain temperature, the hot air balloon experiences a constant upward buoyant force of $F{=}4200\mathrm{N}$. At this point, the anchor is released, and the hot air balloon begins to ascend. During the ascent, the total mass of the hot air balloon (including the mass of the gas inside, the envelope, the gondola, and the heating equipment) remains constant at $m{=}400\mathrm{kg}$. The air resistance $f$ during the ascent is related to the speed $v$ by the equation $f{=}40v$ (both $f$ and $v$ are in SI units). $g$ is taken as $10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. What is the magnitude of the acceleration when a hot air balloon rises at a speed of $2.5\mathrm{m/s}$?
2. What is the magnitude of the constant speed at which the hot air balloon is ascending?

The air inside is heated until the balloon experiences a constant upward buoyant force of $F=4200\mathrm{N}$. The anchor is then released, and the balloon begins to ascend. During the ascent, the total mass of the hot air balloon remains constant at $m=400\mathrm{kg}$. The air resistance is related to the speed $v$ by $f=40v$ (SI units). Take $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$. 1. What is the magnitude of the acceleration when the hot air balloon rises at a speed of $2.5\mathrm{m/s}$? 2. What is the magnitude of the constant speed at which the hot air balloon ascends?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description first: The attached image shows several hot air balloons in an open field, confirming that the physical system is a hot air balloon. The problem concerns the balloon after release, so the relevant motion is vertical ascent. Reasoning: Take upward as positive. The upward buoyant force is F = 4200 N. The mass is m = 400 kg and g = 10 m/s^2, so the weight is mg = 400 × 10 = 4000 N downward. During upward motion, air resistance acts downward with magnitude f = 40v. 1. At v = 2.5 m/s, drag is f = 40 × 2.5 = 100 N. Net force upward is 4200 − 4000 − 100 = 100 N. Therefore a = F_net/m = 100/400 = 0.25 m/s^2, so the acceleration magnitude is 0.25 m/s^2. 2. At constant ascent speed, acceleration is zero, so the net force is zero: 4200 − 4000 − 40v = 0. Thus 40v = 200, giving v = 5 m/s.

raw_record.final_cot:
Image description first: The attached image shows several hot air balloons in an open field, confirming that the physical system is a hot air balloon. The problem concerns the balloon after release, so the relevant motion is vertical ascent.

Reasoning: Take upward as positive. The upward buoyant force is F = 4200 N. The mass is m = 400 kg and g = 10 m/s^2, so the weight is mg = 400 × 10 = 4000 N downward. During upward motion, air resistance acts downward with magnitude f = 40v.

1. At v = 2.5 m/s, drag is f = 40 × 2.5 = 100 N. Net force upward is 4200 − 4000 − 100 = 100 N. Therefore a = F_net/m = 100/400 = 0.25 m/s^2, so the acceleration magnitude is 0.25 m/s^2.

2. At constant ascent speed, acceleration is zero, so the net force is zero: 4200 − 4000 − 40v = 0. Thus 40v = 200, giving v = 5 m/s.
